query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-forming a coherent, Cr-enriched oxide layer on the as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating improves high-temperature wear resistance by blunting the initiation and propagation of both abrasive and adhesive wear mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment using controlled oxygen partial pressure at an elevated temperature to induce the formation of a coherent, adherent oxide layer prior to wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear tests conducted between 300–600 °C under varying loads that simulate both low and high wear regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: A self-forming oxide scale, primarily enriched in chromium (e.g., Cr2O3) and possibly influenced by copper segregation, which acts as a protective, self-healing barrier at the wear interface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact by providing a lubricious and mechanically resilient barrier that mitigates plastic deformation, thereby reducing both abrasive and adhesive wear mechanisms under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit lower wear rates, reduced friction coefficients, and show less spalling or plastic deformation during high-temperature wear tests compared to the untreated (as-deposited) baseline coating.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating without any pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be significant under high-temperature conditions (300–600 °C) with mechanical loads typical of advanced wear testing; outside these temperature and load boundaries, the mechanism may not be operative or may differ.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal oxide thickness and exact composition that maximizes wear resistance, as well as the potential synergistic effects of other alloying elements such as Cu in stabilizing the protective scale.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated samples: one set receives the controlled pre-oxidation treatment and the other remains as-deposited. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature wear tests in the range of 300–600 °C under controlled mechanical loading. Before and after testing, perform detailed surface characterization using SEM and EDS to assess oxide layer continuity, composition, and the presence of wear-induced damage.
measurements: Surface morphology and oxide layer integrity (via SEM imaging)
Chemical composition of the oxide scale (via EDS analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show statistically significant improvements in wear rate and friction coefficient compared to the as-deposited samples, or if the intended stable and protective oxide layer is not observed to form or remain intact during/we after testing, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

AbstractIn order to improve the wear resistance of offshore drilling equipment, CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared by cold spraying (CS) and high-speed oxygen fuel spraying (HVOF), and the coatings were subjected to vacuum heat treatment at different temperatures (500 °C, 700 °C and 900 °C). The friction and wear experiments of the coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment were carried out in simulated seawater drilling fluid. The results show that CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings prepared by CS and HVOF have dense structure and bond well with the substrate. After vacuum heat treatment, the main peaks of all oriented FCC phases are broadened and the peak strength is obviously enhanced. The two types of coatings achieve maximum hardness after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C; the Vickers microhardness of CS-500 °C and HVOF-500 °C are 487.6 and 352.4 HV0.1, respectively. The wear rates of the two coatings at room temperature are very close. CS and HVOF coatings both have the lowest wear rate after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C. frame.goal: To understand and explain the mechanistic origin of its overall wear resistance at high temperatures.
frame.limitation: Prior studies largely focused on room‐temperature wear, coating microstructure (composition and grain size), or limited thermal regimes, rather than the full high-temperature wear response of the coating–substrate system.

the application target is high-temperature wear conditions

frame.understanding:
The hypothesis is that under high-temperature conditions, the overall wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating is governed by the formation and stability of a self-forming, adherent, and protective oxide layer at the wear interface. This oxide layer—enriched in elements such as Cr (and possibly influenced by Cu segregation)—acts to blunt wear mechanisms (both abrasive and adhesive) by providing a dynamic, self-healing barrier that reduces plastic deformation and surface damage. 

Intervention: Modify a baseline coating by pre-oxidizing or thermally aging the surface under controlled oxygen partial pressures to promote the early formation of the protective oxide scale prior to wear testing. 

Predicted Observations: If the hypothesis is correct, the pre-oxidized coating should show a lower wear rate, reduced friction coefficient, and enhanced stability of the worn surface morphology under high-temperature wear tests compared to the untreated baseline coating. Furthermore, under identical high-temperature loads (300–600 °C), the externally induced oxide scale should delay the onset of severe wear modes. 

Connection to Prior Evidence: Previous studies have highlighted the influence of microstructural factors like grain size on wear at room temperature. In many high-temperature applications, however, protective oxide layer formation has been critical in mitigating wear. The current hypothesis links these observations, suggesting that while intrinsic properties set a baseline, the in situ formation of a stable oxide is the dominant mechanism for wear resistance at elevated temperatures. 

Falsification Criterion: The hypothesis would be falsified if, under otherwise identical high-temperature wear test conditions, the intervention (i.e., pre-formed oxide scales) produces no significant improvement—or even degrades—the wear performance compared to the baseline coating. Additionally, if detailed surface analyses reveal that no coherent or protective oxide layer forms during the high-temperature wear tests, this would also refute the proposed mechanism.

decision.trend: Early studies on high‐entropy alloy coatings largely focused on room‐temperature wear behavior by controlling deposition parameters, composition, and microstructural factors such as grain size. Over time, research began exploring how thermal exposure might change the surface properties, leading to incidental formation of oxide scales that improved tribological performance. Notably, in recent work (e.g., PMC10908794), high‐temperature exposure led to the formation of protective oxide and spinel layers on HEA coatings, hinting that high-temperature oxidation can be beneficial. However, these investigations treated the oxide formation as a secondary observation rather than a primary, mechanistic control parameter for wear resistance in a coating–substrate system.
decision.unsolved: How the controlled formation and stability of a protective, self-healing oxide layer at the wear interface governs the overall high-temperature wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating under different mechanical loads. It remains unclear whether pre-forming such oxide scales versus relying on in situ oxidation during wear could offer superior resistance by delaying or mitigating the onset of severe wear modes.
decision.lever: Implement a pre-oxidation treatment using controlled oxygen partial pressures to induce a coherent, adherent oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film prior to high-temperature wear testing.
decision.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that a pre-formed, stable oxide scale can improve high-temperature wear performance by blunting abrasive and adhesive wear mechanisms. It follows logically from previous hints of protective oxide effects seen in high-temperature studies and addresses the identified gap by quantifying the benefit of engineering the oxide layer prior to application.
